rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient that spans nearly the full organic range at a moderate slope and temperature, maximizing the chance that all 10 compounds elute within 42 min while giving a useful first map of the elution window and any critical pairs.

All compounds eluted well within the gradient, so trim the upper organic limit to place the last peak closer to the end of the gradient and spend more gradient time over the actual elution window. This should improve resolution around the crowded 5–8 min region without risking truncation.

The broad window was already fully resolving all 10 compounds, so the main opportunity is to cut time. A steeper version of the successful method will test how much resolution margin we really have while potentially improving CRF through a shorter run.

The 10 min gradient is too steep and compresses the critical 5–7 region, while 20 min had comfortable resolution but a lower CRF from excess time. An intermediate gradient should recover separation of the (5,6)/(6,7) cluster while keeping the run short enough to improve on the current best.

The critical pair improves strongly with shallower slope: R(6,7) rose from 0.46 at 10 min to 1.20 at 14 min and 2.36 at 20 min. A 16 min gradient should push that pair past 1.5 while still keeping the run short enough to target a higher CRF than the 20 min method.

Slope optimization is already tight, so the best remaining lever is temperature to alter selectivity for the critical (6,7) pair without lengthening the run. A 5 C decrease should modestly shift relative retention and may improve that local resolution while keeping runtime near the current optimum.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by creating a new near-coelution, so test the opposite direction at the best time program. A 5 C increase may improve the critical cluster’s selectivity without adding time and could beat the 14 min, 40 C method.

Temperature changes hurt selectivity, so keep 40 C and adjust the solvent window instead. Raising phi0 slightly should shift the crowded early-mid region later into a narrower effective gradient span, potentially improving the critical cluster near rows 5–7 without much time penalty.

The higher starting organic improved CRF while preserving the same critical pair, suggesting this solvent window is better. A slightly longer gradient at the new phi0 should push the 6/7 pair above 1.5 while staying close to the current runtime optimum, with a chance to improve the score further.

The trend from phi0 0.05 to 0.10 was favorable, so push phi0 one more step while keeping the near-optimal gradient time. This may further improve the crowded mid-elution cluster and shave a little runtime, with limited risk since all compounds still elute early.

A perfect CRF has already been reached, so use the remaining budget to test whether the favorable phi0 trend continues while staying in the same successful region. Increasing phi0 another step could retain full resolution and margin while possibly revealing an equally robust alternative optimum.

A perfect method is already in hand, so now probe robustness by trimming the upper end of the window while keeping the successful phi0 and tG. Since the last peak still elutes far before the gradient ends, lowering phi1 may preserve full elution and resolution while confirming whether the broad upper range is unnecessary.

Now test whether the improved phi0 lets us shorten the gradient from the perfect 16 min method without sacrificing too much resolution in the critical 6/7 pair. If resolution stays acceptable, this could reveal another high-scoring, faster alternative near the optimum.

The lower phi1=0.90 run kept full resolution but added a slight time penalty, so test a further trimmed upper window at the proven best phi0 and tG. This checks whether a narrower gradient span can maintain the perfect score region or improve robustness around the critical pair.

A perfect CRF is already achieved, so use this run to map how much extra robustness is gained by a slightly shallower gradient at the best solvent window. This should increase the margin on the critical 6/7 pair and confirm the local optimum shape around the winning method.

The optimum in phi0 and tG is established, so use one remaining probe to test a larger temperature shift for a potentially different selectivity regime. Although ±5 C around 40 C was worse, 25 C could reveal a distinct reordering or separation pattern in the critical cluster that small temperature moves missed.

Since a large drop to 25 C produced a very different and much worse selectivity pattern, run the opposite extreme once to bracket temperature behavior completely. This final temperature boundary test may confirm that the 40 C optimum is robust or unexpectedly reveal a second high-selectivity regime.

With the optimum already found, use a remaining run to define a more conservative backup method centered on the same successful phi window at 40 C. A longer gradient should widen the critical pair further and provide a robust fully resolved alternative if extra resolution margin is desired.

The last peak still elutes early and reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 kept CRF near-perfect, so test a more aggressively trimmed upper window at the best phi0 and tG. This probes how far the gradient range can be narrowed before time penalties outweigh any selectivity benefit.

With the best method already secured, use a remaining injection to fill in the temperature-response map between the poor 25 C and 35 C results. This helps define how sharply selectivity deteriorates below 40 C around the otherwise optimal solvent program.

Complete the temperature map above the optimum by testing the midpoint between 45 and 60 C at the best solvent program. This will show whether selectivity loss with increasing temperature is gradual or whether 40 C is a sharp optimum.

The best method is already secured, so use the remaining budget to complete the slope-response map at the winning solvent window and temperature. A 12 min gradient will better define how rapidly the critical cluster collapses as the gradient is steepened below 14 min.

Only a few injections remain and the optimum is already known, so use one to complete the high-temperature selectivity trend between 50 and 60 C at the best solvent program. This confirms whether loss of resolution above 40 C is monotonic or if any local shoulder exists.

With one of the best non-perfect regions already at phi1 0.90 and another at tG 14, combine them to probe a nearby alternative optimum. This tests whether the slightly narrower window can offset the steeper gradient enough to retain high CRF while shortening the run.

For the final injection, probe the only untested point adjacent to the best-performing region: the successful phi0 0.15, phi1 0.90 window with a slightly shallower gradient. This should increase margin on the critical pair and may match the best score if the time penalty remains negligible.
